To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the graph structure of the Web is very different from the one described in the seminal paper by Broder et.al. (2000) and that it is very different at the different aggregation levels.

(1) the Web is not a power law, (2) it is a giant strongly connected graph, (3) the giant connected component is not the “core” of the Web, and (4) the Web is very different from the “bow tie structure” proposed by Broder et. al. (2000).

(i) the giant strongly connected component is a property of the web graph, but the proportion of nodes that are part of it depends on how the graph is crawled; (ii) the indegree, out degree and strongly connected component size distributions of page and host graphs are not power laws; and (iii) the distance-based features of the web are very different from what has been observed in smaller crawls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of large web graph, and the comparison of its properties at three different levels of granularity: pages, hosts and pay-level domains.
the following questions: (i) what are the properties of the graph structure of the Web? and (ii) how are these properties affected by the level of aggregation?
the analysis of large scale web graphs, and with the understanding of the effects of aggregation on graph properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, as the size of the crawl increases, the graph structure of the Web appears to be less skewed than previously reported.
the structure of the web is very complex and that the structure is dependent on the crawling method and on the level of granularity.
the Web is not a power law, but it is not a power-law-free either.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of the web is very different depending on the granularity at which we analyze it.

the Web is a scale-free network, with a giant strongly connected core, and with a power law distribution of strongly connected components sizes, but that these features are strongly dependent on the level of aggregation.
we find that some features of the web graph that were observed to follow power laws in previous research do not follow a power law in our crawl, but rather a different distribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when analyzing the graph structure of the Web, one should be very cautious about the artifacts introduced by the crawling process.

the graph structure of the Web is strongly dependent on how we aggregate it: the graph structure at the page level is very different from the graph structure at host level, which is in turn very different from the structure at the PLD level.
, in order to obtain accurate measurements of the Web graph, one needs to crawl a large number of pages, and that one has to aggregate at the pay-level domain level.
